node.title: Microbes in Human Welfare: Microbes in household products; Microbes in industrial

lesson.title: Microbes in human welfare: food, industry, sewage, biogas, biocontrol and biofertilisers

coverage.section: Microbes in industrial products: beverages and antibiotics
Microbes in industrial products: beverages and antibiotics
Enzymes and bioactive molecules from microbes

blocks.text: Microbes in household products

Microbes are too small to see, yet we use them every day. The simplest example sits in most kitchens: a spoonful of curd added to warm milk turns it into curd overnight. The bacteria in the starter are **lactic acid bacteria (LAB)**, mainly *Lactobacillus*. They multiply in milk and release lactic acid, which coagulates and partially digests the milk proteins, so the liquid milk sets into a semi-solid curd. Warm surroundings favour their growth, which is why milk sets slowly in winter. Curd is also more nutritious than milk because LAB increase the amount of vitamin B$_{12}$. In the human stomach LAB check the growth of disease-causing microbes.
Bacteria such as *Lactobacillus* that ferment the sugar of milk (lactose) into lactic acid. The acid sets the milk into curd, adds flavour and keeps harmful microbes out.

Other household foods also depend on microbes. The dough used to make bread and the batter used for *dosa* and *idli* are fermented. In bread, baker's yeast (*Saccharomyces cerevisiae*) releases carbon dioxide that puffs up the dough. In the batter of idli and dosa the gas is released by bacteria, and this is what makes the batter rise and gives the softness. Toddy, a traditional drink, is made by fermenting sap from palms. Several fermented foods are made from soaked soya beans, bamboo shoots and fish in different regions.

Cheese is one of the oldest foods made with microbes. Milk is first curdled with bacteria, then the curd is processed and ripened by specific microbes that give each cheese its taste, texture and aroma. The large holes of **Swiss cheese** appear because the bacterium *Propionibacterium sharmanii* produces a large amount of carbon dioxide. The special flavour of **Roquefort cheese** comes from ripening with particular fungi.
Curd: Lactobacillus (LAB), lactic acid, more vitamin B12. Dough: Saccharomyces cerevisiae, CO2. Large holes in Swiss cheese: Propionibacterium sharmanii (CO2). Roquefort cheese: fungal ripening.
Microbes in industrial products: beverages and antibiotics

Industry uses microbes on a very large scale, usually by growing them in huge closed vessels called fermentors or bioreactors. Fermented **beverages** are the oldest industrial product. The yeast *Saccharomyces cerevisiae*, commonly called brewer's yeast, ferments malted cereals and fruit juices to produce ethanol. Wine and beer are produced by fermentation and are **not distilled**, so they have a lower alcohol content. Whisky, brandy and rum are produced by fermentation followed by **distillation**, which gives a higher alcohol content. The raw material decides the drink: grape or other fruit juice gives wine, malted barley gives beer, and different sugar sources give rum and whisky.

A metabolic process in which microbes break down sugars without using oxygen as the final electron acceptor, forming products such as ethanol, carbon dioxide or organic acids. In industry the word is also used loosely for any large-scale microbial production in a fermentor.

**Antibiotics** are chemicals produced by microbes that kill or retard the growth of other, disease-causing microbes ('anti' = against, 'bio' = life). The first antibiotic was found by chance. Alexander Fleming, while working on *Staphylococcus* bacteria, noticed that a mould growing on a contaminated plate had killed the bacteria around it. The mould was *Penicillium notatum* and the substance was **penicillin**. Its full potential as an effective antibiotic was established much later by Ernest Chain and Howard Florey, and Fleming, Chain and Florey shared the Nobel Prize in 1945. Penicillin was widely used to treat wounded soldiers in the Second World War. Many antibiotics have since been discovered, and they have made once-deadly diseases such as plague, whooping cough, diphtheria and leprosy treatable.
Microbes also make **organic acids and alcohol** industrially. The common examples are listed below.
Enzymes and bioactive molecules from microbes
Microbes are also a source of **enzymes** and other **bioactive molecules**, that is, chemicals that act on living systems even in tiny amounts. Some important examples are given below.

blocks.caption: Enzymes and bioactive molecules from microbes
rows: Added to laundry detergents to remove oily stains
Clot buster: dissolves blood clots in the blood vessels of heart-attack patients
Immunosuppressive drug used after organ transplantation
Lower blood cholesterol by competitively inhibiting the enzyme that synthesises cholesterol

blocks.text: Notice that streptokinase and cyclosporin A are not antibiotics. Cyclosporin A does the opposite of fighting germs: it suppresses the immune response so that a transplanted organ is not rejected. Statins act as competitive inhibitors, because their structure resembles the substrate of the cholesterol-synthesising enzyme.

Common mistake: matching the right substance to the wrong microbe. Remember the pairs as sets: streptokinase and Streptococcus (same stem word), cyclosporin and Trichoderma, statins and Monascus, citric acid and Aspergillus, acetic acid and Acetobacter.
Microbes in sewage treatment

Cities produce huge volumes of **sewage**, the waste water carrying human excreta, kitchen and bathroom waste. It is rich in organic matter and disease-causing microbes and must not be released into rivers directly. Sewage is therefore passed through **sewage treatment plants (STPs)** in two stages before release. Microbes do the main work in the second stage.

**Primary treatment** is purely physical. First, floating debris is removed by sequential filtration. Then the grit (soil and small pebbles) is removed by sedimentation. All solids that settle form the **primary sludge**, and the floating material that remains above is the **effluent**. The effluent is taken on to secondary treatment.

**Secondary (biological) treatment**: the primary effluent is passed into large aeration tanks, where it is constantly agitated and air is pumped in. Useful aerobic microbes grow rapidly into masses called **flocs**, which are masses of bacteria held together by slime and fungal filaments to form mesh-like structures. While growing, these microbes consume most of the organic matter in the effluent. This greatly reduces the **biochemical oxygen demand (BOD)** of the effluent.

The amount of oxygen that would be consumed if all the organic matter in one litre of water were oxidised by bacteria. It is a measure of how polluted water is with organic matter: the higher the BOD, the more polluted the water.

When the BOD of the effluent has fallen, it is passed into a settling tank. The flocs settle to the bottom and the sediment is called **activated sludge**. A small part of it is pumped back into the aeration tank as the **inoculum**, to keep the process going. The major part is sent to large tanks called **anaerobic sludge digesters**, where anaerobic bacteria digest the bacteria and fungi of the sludge. During this digestion a mixture of gases (methane, hydrogen sulphide and carbon dioxide) is produced, which forms biogas. The treated effluent from the settling tank is released into rivers or streams.

blocks.problem: A sewage sample entering an aeration tank has a BOD of 300 mg per litre. After secondary treatment the BOD of the effluent is 24 mg per litre. Calculate the percentage reduction in BOD and say which stage is mainly responsible.
blocks.solution: Reduction in BOD = 300 - 24 = 276 mg per litre. Percentage reduction = 276 / 300 x 100 = 92 per cent. The fall in BOD happens in the aeration tank of the secondary treatment, because the aerobic flocs of bacteria and fungal filaments oxidise the organic matter. Primary treatment removes only solids physically and does not lower the BOD of the dissolved matter much.
blocks.answer: 92 per cent reduction; the secondary (biological) treatment, by aerobic microbes in flocs.

blocks.text: Primary treatment = physical (filtration, sedimentation). Secondary treatment = biological (aeration, flocs, BOD falls, activated sludge). Anaerobic sludge digestion gives biogas. A lower BOD means cleaner water.
Production of biogas

**Biogas** is a mixture of gases, mainly **methane** (CH$_4$), with carbon dioxide and a little hydrogen sulphide, produced by microbial action on organic waste in the absence of oxygen. It burns as a fuel. Bacteria called **methanogens** (for example *Methanobacterium*) produce the methane. They live in anaerobic sludge and also in the **rumen** (a part of the stomach) of cattle, where they help in the breakdown of cellulose-rich plant material. This is why cattle dung (gobar) is an excellent raw material, and biogas is called **gobar gas** in India.

The process runs in a biogas plant, a concrete tank of 10 to 15 feet depth, into which a slurry of dung is fed. A floating cover on top rises as gas collects. The gas is drawn off through an outlet pipe for cooking and lighting, and the spent slurry is removed through another outlet and used as manure. The technology was developed in India mainly by the Indian Agricultural Research Institute (IARI) and the Khadi and Village Industries Commission (KVIC).

blocks.problem: Explain, step by step, how an anaerobic digester converts cattle dung into usable fuel, and name the organisms and the main gas.
blocks.solution: Step 1: dung is mixed with water into a slurry and fed into the digester. Step 2: because there is no oxygen, anaerobic bacteria first break down the complex cellulose and other organic matter into simple compounds. Step 3: methanogens such as Methanobacterium then convert these into methane, along with carbon dioxide and a little hydrogen sulphide. Step 4: the gas collects under the floating cover and is taken out as fuel, while the residue is used as manure.
blocks.answer: Methanogens produce biogas, whose main gas is methane.

blocks.text: Microbes as biocontrol agents

Biocontrol means using living organisms to control pests and diseases instead of chemical pesticides, which pollute the soil and water and harm useful organisms. Classical examples are the **ladybird beetle**, which feeds on aphids, and the **dragonfly**, which eats mosquitoes. In modern organic farming the following microbes are used.

*Bacillus thuringiensis* (**Bt**) is sold as sachets of dried spores. The spores are mixed with water and sprayed on vulnerable plants such as brassicas and fruit trees, where they are eaten by insect larvae. In the gut of the larva the toxin is released and kills it, while the bacterium is harmless to the plant. Bt genes have also been inserted into crops to make Bt cotton. *Trichoderma* is a free-living fungus found in root ecosystems and is a biocontrol agent for several plant diseases. **Baculoviruses**, such as the nucleopolyhedrovirus (NPV), attack insects and other arthropods. They are species-specific and have a narrow spectrum of action, with no negative effect on plants, mammals, birds, fish or even non-target insects, so they are ideal for integrated pest management (IPM) in an ecologically sensitive area.

Exam tip: Bt is a bacterium, Trichoderma is a fungus and baculovirus is a virus. All three are used as biocontrol agents. A frequent distractor is to call baculovirus a broad-spectrum pesticide; it is the opposite, being highly specific.
Microbes as biofertilisers

**Biofertilisers** are living organisms that enrich the nutrient quality of the soil. The main sources are bacteria, fungi and cyanobacteria. They reduce the need for chemical fertilisers and are a key part of organic farming.

The nodules on the roots of leguminous plants such as peas and beans are formed by the symbiotic association of *Rhizobium* with the roots. The bacterium fixes atmospheric nitrogen into organic forms that the plant can use. Other bacteria, such as *Azospirillum* and *Azotobacter*, are free-living and fix atmospheric nitrogen in the soil, enriching its nitrogen content. **Mycorrhiza** is a symbiotic association of a fungus with the roots of higher plants; many members of the genus *Glomus* form it. The fungal filaments absorb phosphorus from the soil and pass it to the plant. Plants with this association show resistance to root-borne pathogens, tolerance to salinity and drought, and an overall increase in growth and development. **Cyanobacteria** such as *Anabaena*, *Nostoc* and *Oscillatoria* are autotrophic microbes widely distributed in aquatic and terrestrial environments, and many of them can fix atmospheric nitrogen. In paddy fields cyanobacteria are an important biofertiliser, and they also add organic matter to the soil and increase its fertility.

blocks.caption: Biofertilisers at a glance
rows: Fixes nitrogen in root nodules of legumes
Absorbs phosphorus, protects against pathogens, drought and salinity
Fix nitrogen, mainly in paddy fields

blocks.problem: Classify each of the following as bacterium, fungus or virus and state the human-welfare use: (i) Lactobacillus, (ii) Penicillium notatum, (iii) Nucleopolyhedrovirus, (iv) Glomus.
blocks.solution: (i) Lactobacillus is a bacterium: it turns milk into curd and increases vitamin B12. (ii) Penicillium notatum is a fungus (a mould): it produces the antibiotic penicillin. (iii) Nucleopolyhedrovirus is a baculovirus, so it is a virus: it is a species-specific biocontrol agent used against insect pests. (iv) Glomus is a fungus: it forms mycorrhiza with roots and supplies phosphorus to the plant.
blocks.answer: (i) bacterium, curd; (ii) fungus, penicillin; (iii) virus, biocontrol; (iv) fungus, biofertiliser.

blocks.text: Microbes feed us (curd, bread, cheese, drinks), heal us (antibiotics, streptokinase, cyclosporin A, statins), clean our water (sewage treatment), give fuel (biogas) and protect and nourish crops (biocontrol and biofertilisers).

Last-minute revision: keep a list of microbe-product pairs, and remember that wine and beer are not distilled while whisky, brandy and rum are. Never confuse BOD with a measure of oxygen present; it is oxygen demanded.

questions.stem: Which microbe is mainly responsible for converting milk into curd?
questions.explanation: Curd is formed by lactic acid bacteria such as Lactobacillus. They ferment lactose into lactic acid, which coagulates and partially digests the milk proteins. Yeast makes bread dough rise, Penicillium makes penicillin and Rhizobium fixes nitrogen.

optionRationale.1: Saccharomyces is baker's and brewer's yeast, used for dough and ethanol, not for curd.
optionRationale.3: Penicillium notatum is a mould that yields penicillin.
optionRationale.4: Rhizobium forms root nodules in legumes and fixes nitrogen.

questions.objective: Identify the microbe used to make curd

questions.stem: The large holes in Swiss cheese are due to the production of a large amount of carbon dioxide by
questions.explanation: Swiss cheese gets its large holes because Propionibacterium sharmanii gives off a lot of carbon dioxide during ripening. Roquefort cheese, in contrast, is flavoured by specific fungi, and Acetobacter aceti produces acetic acid, not gas holes in cheese.

optionRationale.1: Lactobacillus makes curd, not the holes in Swiss cheese.
optionRationale.2: A fungus is used for the flavour of Roquefort cheese, not for the holes in Swiss cheese.

questions.objective: Recall the microbe behind Swiss cheese holes

questions.stem: Wine and beer are produced by fermentation, whereas whisky, brandy and rum need one more step. That step is
questions.explanation: Wine and beer are not distilled and so have a lower alcohol content. Whisky, brandy and rum are produced by fermentation followed by distillation, which raises the alcohol content. Aeration and sedimentation are steps of sewage treatment.

optionRationale.1: Aeration is a step of sewage treatment, not of liquor production.
optionRationale.3: Sedimentation is used in the primary treatment of sewage.
optionRationale.4: Filtration only removes particles and does not increase alcohol content.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a clot-buster used to remove blood clots from the vessels of heart-attack patients?
questions.explanation: Streptokinase, produced by the bacterium Streptococcus and modified for use, dissolves clots in blood vessels and is called a clot buster. Cyclosporin A suppresses the immune system, statins lower blood cholesterol and lipases are used in detergents.

optionRationale.1: Cyclosporin A is an immunosuppressant used after organ transplantation.
optionRationale.2: Statins lower blood cholesterol and do not dissolve clots.
optionRationale.3: Lipases remove oily stains in detergents.

questions.objective: Match a bioactive molecule with its function

questions.stem: In a sewage treatment plant, flocs are formed during
options: primary treatment, in the sedimentation tank
secondary treatment, in the aeration tank
the release of treated effluent into a river
questions.explanation: Flocs are masses of bacteria held together with fungal filaments. They grow during secondary treatment, when the effluent is aerated in large tanks, and they oxidise the organic matter. Primary treatment is only physical, and the digester contains anaerobic organisms that digest the sludge.

optionRationale.1: Primary treatment removes solids physically and no biological flocs grow there.
optionRationale.3: In the anaerobic digester flocs are digested, not formed.
optionRationale.4: Release into a river is the final step after treatment.

questions.objective: Locate floc formation in the treatment sequence

questions.stem:
Assertion (A): The biochemical oxygen demand of sewage falls greatly after secondary treatment.
Reason (R): Aerobic microbes in the flocs consume most of the organic matter of the effluent in the aeration tank.
options: Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).
questions.explanation: BOD measures the oxygen that bacteria would need to oxidise all organic matter in the water. In the aeration tank the aerobic microbes of the flocs consume the organic matter, so there is much less left to oxidise and the BOD falls. The reason therefore directly explains the assertion.

optionRationale.2: R is a correct explanation, not merely an unrelated true statement: the microbes consume the organic matter that creates oxygen demand.
optionRationale.3: A is true, because BOD falls sharply after the aeration stage.
optionRationale.4: R is true, because aerobic microbes in flocs do consume the organic matter in the aeration tank.

questions.objective: Explain why secondary treatment lowers BOD

questions.stem: Match the products in List-I with the microbes in List-II.
questions.explanation: Citric acid is made by the fungus Aspergillus niger, acetic acid by Acetobacter aceti, butyric acid by Clostridium butylicum and cyclosporin A by the fungus Trichoderma polysporum. This gives A-III, B-I, C-IV, D-II, which is the first option.

optionRationale.2: This option pairs citric acid with Acetobacter, which makes acetic acid.
optionRationale.3: This option pairs citric acid with Trichoderma and butyric acid with Aspergillus, both wrong.
optionRationale.4: This option pairs citric acid with Clostridium, which makes butyric acid.

questions.objective: Match industrial products with their microbes

questions.stem:
Consider the following statements about microbes as biocontrol agents.
A. Baculoviruses are species-specific and have a narrow spectrum of insecticidal action.
B. Spores of Bacillus thuringiensis are sprayed on plants and kill larvae that eat them.
C. Trichoderma is a bacterium used to control insects.
Choose the correct option.
questions.explanation: Statements A and B are correct. Baculoviruses (such as NPV) attack only particular insects, and Bt spores sprayed on crops release a toxin in the gut of the larvae. Statement C is wrong because Trichoderma is a fungus that controls plant diseases, not a bacterium that controls insects.

optionRationale.2: Statement C is false, so B and C cannot both be accepted.
optionRationale.3: Statement C is false because Trichoderma is a fungus, so A and C is wrong.
optionRationale.4: Statement C is false, so all three cannot be correct.

questions.stem: The BOD of a sewage sample is 240 mg per litre before treatment and it is reduced by 85 per cent by secondary treatment. The BOD of the treated effluent is
questions.explanation: A reduction of 85 per cent leaves 15 per cent of the original BOD. 15 per cent of 240 is 0.15 x 240 = 36 mg per litre. The value 204 is the amount removed, not what is left.

optionRationale.2: 85 is the percentage figure itself and not the remaining BOD.
optionRationale.3: 204 mg per litre is the reduction (0.85 x 240), not what remains.
optionRationale.4: 155 comes from subtracting 85 from 240, which wrongly treats the percentage as mg per litre.

questions.objective: Calculate residual BOD from percentage reduction

questions.stem: Which of the following biofertilisers is an autotrophic microbe that fixes nitrogen in paddy fields?
questions.explanation: Anabaena is a cyanobacterium, which is autotrophic because it carries out photosynthesis, and many cyanobacteria fix atmospheric nitrogen in paddy fields. Glomus is a fungus for phosphorus uptake, Azotobacter is a free-living heterotrophic bacterium and Rhizobium is symbiotic in legume roots.

optionRationale.1: Glomus is a mycorrhizal fungus that helps in phosphorus absorption.
optionRationale.2: Azotobacter is a free-living bacterium and not a photosynthetic cyanobacterium.
optionRationale.3: Rhizobium works in the root nodules of legumes, not in paddy water.

questions.stem:
Assertion (A): Methane is produced in an anaerobic sludge digester and in the rumen of cattle.
Reason (R): Methanogens such as Methanobacterium are strict aerobes that need oxygen to form methane.
options: Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).
questions.explanation: The assertion is true because methanogens live in anaerobic sludge and in the rumen, where cellulose is digested. The reason is false because methanogens are anaerobic and form methane only in the absence of oxygen. So A is true and R is false.

optionRationale.1: R is false, so it cannot be a correct explanation.
optionRationale.2: R is false, so the pair cannot both be true.
optionRationale.4: A is true, not false, as methane is made in both places.

questions.objective: Detect the false reason about methanogens

questions.stem:
Consider the following statements about sewage treatment.
A. Primary treatment removes floating debris by sequential filtration and grit by sedimentation.
B. A small part of the activated sludge is pumped back into the aeration tank as inoculum.
C. The major part of the activated sludge is discarded without further digestion.
D. Anaerobic digestion of sludge forms a mixture of methane, hydrogen sulphide and carbon dioxide.
Which statements are correct?
questions.explanation: A, B and D are correct. The major part of the activated sludge goes to anaerobic sludge digesters, so statement C is wrong. Digestion there forms biogas, a mixture of methane, hydrogen sulphide and carbon dioxide, and a small part is recycled as inoculum.

optionRationale.1: C is false because the major part goes to digesters, not to discard.
optionRationale.2: C is false, so any option that contains it is wrong.
optionRationale.3: C is false, and this option also leaves out the correct statement A.

questions.objective: Evaluate statements on sewage treatment steps

questions.stem: A farmer wants an insect-specific control for a pest on a vegetable crop with minimum harm to birds, fish and non-target insects. Which choice is the most suitable?
questions.explanation: Baculoviruses such as NPV are species-specific with a narrow spectrum and have no negative effect on plants, mammals, birds, fish or non-target insects, making them ideal for integrated pest management. A chemical insecticide is broad-spectrum, Azospirillum is a nitrogen-fixing biofertiliser and streptokinase is a drug.

optionRationale.1: A broad-spectrum chemical insecticide kills many non-target organisms and pollutes the environment.
optionRationale.3: Azospirillum fixes nitrogen and does not control pests.
optionRationale.4: Streptokinase is a medicine and has no use as an insecticide.

questions.objective: Choose a suitable biocontrol agent for a situation

questions.stem: Match the microbial substance in List-I with its use in List-II.

right: II. Removing oily stains in detergents

questions.explanation: Streptokinase dissolves blood clots, so A matches with III. Statins lower blood cholesterol, so B matches with IV. Lipases are used in detergents, so C matches with II. Pectinases clarify bottled juices, so D matches with I. That gives A-III, B-IV, C-II, D-I.

optionRationale.1: This pairs streptokinase with detergent use, which is for lipases.
optionRationale.2: This pairs streptokinase with juice clarification, which is for pectinases.
optionRationale.4: This pairs streptokinase with lowering cholesterol, which is for statins.

questions.objective: Match enzymes and bioactive molecules with applications

questions.stem: During sewage treatment, the BOD of the effluent was found to be very high just before aeration and very low after the settling of flocs. Which statement best explains this?
options: Anaerobic bacteria in the sludge digester consumed the oxygen of the effluent
Aerobic microbes of the flocs oxidised the organic matter in the aerated effluent
Sedimentation removed all dissolved gases from the effluent
Primary sludge was recycled into the effluent as inoculum
questions.explanation: BOD falls when organic matter is removed. In the aeration tank, aerobic microbes in the flocs oxidise the organic matter, and the flocs then settle as activated sludge, leaving effluent with low BOD. Anaerobic digestion happens in a separate tank for the sludge, and the inoculum is activated sludge, not primary sludge.

optionRationale.1: The anaerobic digester treats sludge, in a separate tank, and does not lower the BOD of the effluent in the aeration tank.
optionRationale.3: Sedimentation removes solids, not dissolved gases, and does not explain the fall in BOD.
optionRationale.4: The inoculum is a small part of activated sludge, not primary sludge, and recycling does not remove organic matter.

questions.objective: Interpret a change in BOD during treatment
